content: CD45, also known as the leukocyte common antigen, is a protein that plays a critical role in the immune system. It is a member of the protein tyrosine phosphatase (PTP) family, which consists of signaling molecules that regulate various cellular processes, including cell growth, differentiation, the mitotic cycle, and oncogenic transformation. CD45 is classified as a receptor-type PTP because it contains an extracellular domain, a single transmembrane segment, and two tandem intracytoplasmic catalytic domains. This protein is specifically expressed in hematopoietic cells and is essential for the regulation of T-cell and B-cell antigen receptor signaling. It achieves this by either directly interacting with components of the antigen receptor complexes or by activating various Src family kinases that are necessary for antigen receptor signaling. Additionally, CD45 suppresses JAK kinases, thereby acting as a regulator of cytokine receptor signaling. CD45 is a type I transmembrane protein that is expressed in various forms on all differentiated hematopoietic cells, except for erythrocytes and plasma cells. It plays a role in the activation of these cells, functioning as a co-stimulatory molecule. CD45 expression is observed in lymphomas, B-cell chronic lymphocytic leukemia, hairy cell leukemia, and acute nonlymphocytic leukemia. The CD45 family is composed of multiple members, all of which are products of a single complex gene. This gene contains 34 exons, and three of these exons are alternatively spliced to produce up to eight different mature mRNAs. These mRNAs are translated into eight distinct protein isoforms. The three alternatively spliced exons generate the RA, RB, and RC isoforms. The various isoforms of CD45 include CD45RA, CD45RB, CD45RC, CD45RAB, CD45RAC, CD45RBC, CD45RO, and CD45R(ABC). CD45 is highly glycosylated, and its isoforms differ in molecular weight due to variations in glycosylation. CD45R is the longest isoform, migrating at 200 kDa when isolated from T cells. In B cells, CD45R undergoes heavier glycosylation, resulting in a molecular weight of 220 kDa, which is referred to as B220. Interestingly, B220 expression is not limited to B cells; it can also be found on activated T cells, a subset of dendritic cells, and other antigen-presenting cells. Naive T lymphocytes predominantly express the larger CD45 isoforms, such as CD45RA. In contrast, activated and memory T lymphocytes express the shortest isoform, CD45RO, which lacks the RA, RB, and RC exons. This shorter isoform is particularly important for facilitating T-cell activation. The cytoplasmic domain of CD45 is one of the largest known among proteins and possesses intrinsic phosphatase activity. This activity is crucial for removing an inhibitory phosphate group from tyrosine kinases such as Lck in T cells or Syk in B cells, thereby activating these kinases and promoting downstream signaling events.
